books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Uncle Sam’s Youngest Son, Citizen Know Nothing (Sarony & Co., lithograph, New York, 1854). Library of Congress, LCCN2003689281. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A lithograph published in New York in 1854, titled “Uncle Sam’s Youngest Son, Citizen Know Nothing.” It shows a young man in a wide-brimmed hat, wrapped in an American flag, with a plaque reading “CITIZEN” below him and an eagle above.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note

parts.prompt: Identify one feature of the cartoon that presents the Know-Nothing as a true American.
parts.modelAnswer: The young man is wrapped in the American flag and titled “Uncle Sam’s Youngest Son,” with the word “CITIZEN” stamped below him. The flag and the title present him as a native-born American, the truest kind of citizen.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for identifying one feature, such as the flag, the title, or the word “CITIZEN,” that presents the figure as a true American.
scoring.notEarned: Describing the cartoon with no feature tied to American identity does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain why Irish and German immigration in the 1840s and 1850s provoked a nativist reaction.
parts.modelAnswer: Millions of Irish and German immigrants arrived in those decades, settling in Northern cities and keeping their Catholic faith and languages. Native-born Protestants feared the newcomers’ numbers and customs, and they organized to limit immigrant rights and political power.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining why the immigration wave provoked nativism, with at least one specific detail such as the newcomers’ numbers, Catholic faith, or city settlement.
scoring.notEarned: Naming immigration with no explanation of the nativist reaction does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain one political consequence of the Know-Nothing movement in the 1850s.
parts.modelAnswer: The Know-Nothing Party, formally the American Party, won elections in several states, especially in the Northeast, in the 1850s. Its rise showed that nativism could win votes, and many Know-Nothings later joined the new Republican Party.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one political consequence, such as Know-Nothing electoral wins or members joining the Republican Party.
scoring.notEarned: Naming the party with no consequence does not earn the point.
